passages.t: Who is the greatest? Become like a child
passages.happening:
The disciples come to Jesus with a question: “Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” (verse 1). Jesus calls a little child and has the child stand among them.

“Truly I tell you,” he says, “unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (verse 3). Whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom. And whoever welcomes a little child like this in Jesus' name welcomes him.
passages.hearers:
This is the fourth of the five long blocks of teaching in Matthew. Its subject is how Jesus' followers are to live together. It ends, like the others, with the words ‘When Jesus had finished saying these things’ (19:1).

Mark tells how the disciples argued on the road about which of them was the greatest, and went quiet when Jesus asked (Mark 9:33-34). The note on Mark 9 tells that story. In Matthew they ask Jesus straight out. Either way, the question is about rank.

The answer turns on what a child was in that world. Children were loved by their parents, but they had no rank. They could not earn, vote, give orders or pay anyone back. Greek even used one word, pais, for a child and for a servant. So ‘become like little children’ is not about being sweet or innocent. It is about status. A child has no claim to greatness and does not pretend to one. A child depends on others and receives.

‘Change’ is literally ‘turn’. It is a turning around, away from the contest for first place. And ‘humbles himself’ is the same family of words Jesus uses of himself: “I am gentle and humble in heart” (11:29). The greatest in the kingdom look like the king.
passages.ot: The prophets said God cares most for the weakest of his flock: “He gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart” (Isaiah 40:11). And the Scriptures promise that God lifts up the lowly. Jesus makes that the rule of rank in his kingdom.
passages.asks: The disciples wanted to know where they stood. Jesus set before them someone who stood nowhere. Ask where you are still keeping score of your own place among other Christians. Then ask who, in your church, has no rank at all, and how you could welcome them as you would welcome Jesus.

passages.t: Causing a little one to stumble
passages.happening:
Jesus gives a fierce warning. If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in him to stumble, “it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea” (verse 6). Things that cause people to fall will come in this world. But woe to the one through whom they come.

Then he turns the warning inward. If your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. If your eye causes you to sin, gouge it out. It is better to enter life with one hand or one eye than to be thrown whole into the fire of hell.
passages.hearers:
‘Causes to stumble’ is one Greek word, skandalizō. The noun, skandalon, was a trap or an obstacle in the road, something that trips a person and brings them down. Jesus had just used the word for not putting a stumbling block in the way of the tax collectors (17:27). Here the danger is far worse: leading a believer away from faith, or wounding them so badly that they fall.

‘These little ones’ means children, like the child standing among them, and also every weak or young believer. Jesus used the same words for his humble followers in 10:42.

The millstone, the note on Mark 9 explains, is literally a ‘donkey millstone’, the great upper stone of a mill turned by an animal. Tied to a neck, it meant certain drowning.

‘Hell’ here is Gehenna, from the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem. There, in Judah's worst days, people had burned their own children as sacrifices (Jeremiah 7:31). A valley where children were killed became the name for God's final judgment. Jesus uses that name in a passage about protecting children.

The words about the hand, the foot and the eye repeat what Jesus said in 5:29-30, now in a new setting. There they were about lust. Here they come right after the warning about harming the little ones.
passages.ot: The fire that is never put out comes from the last lines of Isaiah: “their worm will never die, their fire will never be quenched” (Isaiah 66:24). And the Law commanded care for those who could easily be made to fall: “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14).
passages.hard:
These words have been rightly applied to the abuse of children. It must be said plainly. This passage stands with the child. Jesus' fiercest warning in the Gospels is for anyone who harms a little one. The church has sometimes protected abusers and silenced children, and that is a betrayal of this very passage. Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault.

Does Jesus want people to cut off their hands or put out their eyes? No. He is using a strong picture, as teachers in his culture often did, to show how serious sin is. The point is to cut off whatever leads you into sin, a habit, a place, a relationship, a screen, however much it costs. The church has always taught that this is not a command to harm the body. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone now: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line.

On hell itself, Christians agree that Jesus warned of real and final judgment. They differ on what that judgment is like, and these notes do not settle that here.
passages.asks: Jesus speaks most fiercely about those who make the weak fall. Ask whether anything in your life, your words, your example or your anger, makes it harder for someone young in faith to trust Jesus. And ask whether your church is a place where a child who has been hurt would be believed and protected.

passages.happening:
“See that you do not look down on any of these little ones,” Jesus says. “For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father in heaven” (verse 10).

Then a story. If a man has a hundred sheep and one goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go to search for the one? If he finds it, he is happier over that one than over the ninety-nine that did not wander. “In the same way, your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish” (verse 14).

Your Bible may go straight from verse 10 to verse 12. That is explained below.
passages.hearers:
To ‘see the face’ of a king meant to have access to him, to stand in his presence and have his ear. So the little ones whom people look down on have angels who stand before the Father. The weakest believer is not unknown in heaven. Many Jews of Jesus' day believed God appointed angels to watch over people, and the believers in Acts, hearing Peter at the door, said, “It must be his angel” (Acts 12:15). From this verse comes the Christian idea of guardian angels. Christians differ over how far it teaches an angel for each person. Its point here is plain: no one may treat a little one as if they did not matter.

Luke tells the lost sheep too, but in a different setting (Luke 15:3-7). There Jesus tells it to Pharisees who grumble that he welcomes sinners, and the sheep is ‘lost’. Here he tells it to his disciples, and the sheep ‘goes astray’, a word Matthew also uses for being led astray by false teachers (24:4-5). In Luke, the shepherd searches ‘until he finds it’. In Matthew, it is ‘if he finds it’. So in Matthew the story is a charge to the church: do not let a wandering believer go.

Verse 11. Older Bibles, such as the King James Version, have a verse here: ‘For the Son of Man came to save that which was lost.’ The oldest copies of Matthew, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus among them, do not have it. Most scholars think a copyist brought it in from Luke 19:10, where Jesus says, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” So the BSB leaves the number 11 empty. The truth it states is plain in Luke.
passages.ot: The story echoes Ezekiel 34. There God rebukes Israel's shepherds, because “My flock went astray on all the mountains and every high hill” with no one to look for them (Ezekiel 34:6). Then God promises to be the shepherd himself: “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak” (Ezekiel 34:16). The angels who watch over God's people recall the psalm: “For He will command His angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways” (Psalm 91:11).
passages.asks: The ninety-nine are safe. The shepherd's heart is with the one who is not. Ask who has drifted away from your church or your circle without anyone going after them. And if you are the one who has wandered, hear verse 14 as meant for you.

passages.t: When a brother sins: tell it to the church
passages.happening:
“If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over” (verse 15).

If he will not listen, take one or two others with you, so that every matter may be established by two or three witnesses. If he will not listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he will not listen even to the church, “regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The first step is private. Not gossip, not a public charge, but a quiet word to the person, face to face. And the goal is stated at once: ‘you have won your brother over.’ The aim is to win a person back, not to win an argument.

Jewish communities of the time had rules like this. The Community Rule, one of the Dead Sea Scrolls, told a member to correct his fellow in truth and humility, and not to bring a charge before the whole community unless he had first corrected him before witnesses.

‘Church’ here is the Greek word ekklēsia, the gathered assembly. In the Gospels it appears only twice, in 16:18 and here. Here it means the local gathering of believers.

‘Regard him as a pagan or a tax collector.’ Pagans, or Gentiles, and tax collectors stood outside the life of Israel's community. So the words mean that a person who will not listen even to the whole church is no longer treated as a member in good standing. But notice how Jesus treated tax collectors. He called one, Matthew, to follow him (9:9). He ate with them, and was called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (11:19). Matthew, who wrote these words, had been a tax collector himself. So these words do not give anyone leave for contempt or cruelty. They change the relationship. The person is now someone outside, to be sought and won again.
passages.ot: Jesus builds on the Law. Leviticus says, “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. Directly rebuke your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:17), and the next verse forbids revenge and grudges. The rule about witnesses is Deuteronomy 19:15: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” And that same chapter sends a disputed case to judges who “shall investigate thoroughly” (Deuteronomy 19:18).
passages.hard:
This passage has been badly misused, and that must be faced. Matthew 18 is not a rule that makes a harmed person meet the one who harmed them. It opens by placing Christ's presence in a child, “whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me” (Matthew 18:5), and by warning of the millstone. Nothing in it asks a child, or anyone who is afraid, to go alone to the person who hurt them. The law behind the two or three witnesses sends a disputed case to judges who “shall investigate thoroughly” (Deuteronomy 19:18), so it's no excuse for refusing to look. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). Nothing in verses 15 to 20 puts a church meeting in the place of the police.

The steps Jesus gives are for wrongs between believers who stand on roughly equal ground. They do not fit a case where one person has power over another, or where someone is afraid. Nor are they a way to silence someone who raises a concern by telling them, ‘You did not go to him first.’

How should a church practise verse 17? Churches have answered in different ways. Some can keep a person from Communion for a time, hoping to bring them back. Some practise church discipline carried out by elders, and some by the whole congregation. Others use little formal discipline and rely on pastoral care. All take their lead from passages such as this and Paul's letters, which aim at restoring the person: “restore him with a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1), and later, “forgive and comfort him” (2 Corinthians 2:7). These notes do not choose among the churches' practices.
passages.asks: Jesus sends you to the person, not to everyone else about the person. Ask whether there is someone you have talked about rather than talked to. If it is safe, what would a quiet first step look like? If it is not safe, that is not what this passage asks of you.

passages.t: Bound in heaven; two or three in My name
passages.happening: Jesus goes on: whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. If two of you on earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by my Father in heaven. “For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
‘Bind’ and ‘loose’ were the words Jewish teachers used for forbidding and permitting. The note on 16:19 explains them. There Jesus spoke the words to Peter. Here he gives them to the disciples together, the gathered church.

Read verses 19 and 20 where they stand. They come straight after the steps for dealing with a brother who sins. The ‘two or three’ are the same two or three witnesses of verse 16. The ‘two of you’ who agree are the church weighing a hard matter and asking God for wisdom. Jesus promises that when they gather in his name to do that hard work, he is in the room.

That is why the promise is so strong. It is not mainly about small prayer meetings, though Jesus is present there too. It is about the hardest moments in a church's life: naming sin, deciding with fear and care, and praying over a broken relationship.

Later Jewish teachers said something similar of the Law. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, gives a saying of Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion: when two sit together and the words of the Law pass between them, God's presence rests among them (Avot 3:2). Jesus says that where two or three gather in his name, he is there. He puts himself where the teachers put God's presence.
passages.ot: Matthew's whole Gospel is framed by this promise. At the start, Jesus is called Immanuel, which means “God with us” (1:23). At the end, he says, “And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (28:20). In the middle, here, he promises to stand among his gathered people. God's presence among his people runs through the whole of Scripture, from the tabernacle in the desert to the temple. Now it is found where his people meet in his name.
passages.hard: Does verse 19 mean that whatever any two Christians agree to ask for, God must give? Read in its place, it is a promise about the church seeking God's will in a hard case, not a technique for getting what we want. Jesus himself prayed in the garden, “Yet not as I will, but as You will” (26:39). Prayer agreed together is powerful, and Jesus delights to answer. But no verse turns God into a machine that gives on demand.
passages.asks: The promise of Jesus' presence was given for the hard room, not only the warm one. Ask when you last prayed with one or two others over a wound in your church or your family. And when you gather in his name, remember who else is there.

passages.t: Seventy-seven times, and the servant who would not forgive
passages.happening:
Peter asks, “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother who sins against me? Up to seven times?” (verse 21). Jesus answers, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!” (verse 22).

Then he tells a story. A king settles accounts with his servants. One owes him ten thousand talents. He cannot pay, so the king orders that he, his wife, his children and all he has be sold. The servant falls on his knees: ‘Have patience with me, and I will pay back everything.’ The king has compassion, cancels the whole debt and lets him go.

That servant goes out and finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii. He grabs him by the throat: “Pay back what you owe me!” The man falls down and begs with almost the same words: ‘Have patience with me, and I will pay you back.’ But he refuses and has the man thrown into prison.

The other servants are greatly distressed and tell the king. The king calls him in: “You wicked servant! I forgave all your debt because you begged me. Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?” In anger the king hands him over to the jailers until he repays all he owes. “That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Peter thinks he is being generous. Seven is a full, round number. Later Jewish teaching set a smaller limit. A saying in the Babylonian Talmud, written down several centuries after Jesus, teaches that a person who sins is forgiven a first, second and third time, but not a fourth (Yoma 86b). Jesus does not raise Peter's number. He ends the counting.

Is it seventy-seven times, or seventy times seven? The Greek can be read either way. Older Bibles, such as the King James Version, say ‘seventy times seven’. Many modern Bibles, such as the BSB, say ‘seventy-seven’, because the same Greek words are used in the Greek Old Testament for Lamech's boast in Genesis 4:24. The point is the same either way: forgiveness is not a ration to be counted.

Then the numbers in the story. A talent was the largest sum of money anyone reckoned in, worth about six thousand denarii, and a denarius was a day's pay for a labourer (20:2). Ten thousand talents is sixty million days' pay. No servant could ever earn it. To give a sense of scale, the historian Josephus says the yearly tax from all of Galilee and Perea, paid to Herod Antipas, came to two hundred talents (Antiquities 17.318). The servant owed fifty times that. Jesus' hearers would have heard a debt beyond counting.

The fellow servant's hundred denarii was about a hundred days' pay. Real money, but next to the first debt, a speck.

Listen to the two pleas. They are almost the same words (verses 26 and 29). The forgiven servant hears his own prayer in another man's mouth, and does not recognize it.
passages.ot:
Jesus' ‘seventy-seven’ answers an old song of revenge. Lamech, a descendant of Cain, boasted, “If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (Genesis 4:24). Revenge without limit is answered by forgiveness without limit.

A debt so large was a known figure. When Haman plotted to destroy the Jews, he offered the king “ten thousand talents of silver” (Esther 3:9).

Selling a debtor's family was a real fear in Israel too. A widow cried to Elisha that “his creditor is coming to take my two children as his slaves” (2 Kings 4:1). But the Law limited such debts and released Israelites in the Year of Jubilee (Leviticus 25:39-40). Many readers think the king's harsh orders, the selling, the prison and the jailers, sound more like the courts of foreign kings.
passages.hard:
Does verse 35 mean we earn God's forgiveness by forgiving others? Most Christian traditions say no. In this parable the king cancels the servant's huge debt first and freely. The servant is condemned because he refuses to pass on the mercy he received (verse 33). Forgiving others is the sign that God's forgiveness has really reached us, not the price of it. A heart that holds on to every debt has not let God's mercy in. Christians do differ on what the warning means for a believer. Some hold that a person who goes on refusing mercy can lose the grace they received. Others hold that such a person shows they were never truly changed. All agree the warning is meant to be heard.

Nor is the king a picture of God as cruel. A parable makes one point, and the details serve it. The point here is the gap between a mercy without limit and a heart that will not pass it on.

Forgiveness has also been misused. Some have told people who were abused to forgive quickly, keep quiet, or go back to the person who hurt them. That is not what this parable asks. Forgiveness lets go of revenge. It is not the same as trusting someone again, and it does not mean a crime should go unreported. A person can forgive and still stay safe, still tell the truth, and still ask for justice. It can also take a long time, and that is not failure.

Forgiving from the heart is not the same as trusting again, reconciling, or keeping quiet. Making peace takes two, and Luke records Jesus' words, “If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him” (Luke 17:3). If someone has harmed you, tell someone safe, and if a crime was committed, go to the police. You don't need anyone's permission to be safe.
passages.asks: Think of the debt you have been forgiven. It is the ten thousand talents. Then ask whose hundred denarii you are still holding. You may need time, and help, to let it go, and that is not failure. But ask God to let the mercy that reached you begin to reach them.
